fixes.explanation: Livestock is it, baker. These two tribes had very large herds and flocks, and they saw that Jazer and Gilead were suitable for livestock (Numbers 32:1). When you own that many animals, every open stretch of land looks like a place to put them. I do the same thing with a bare counter and a fresh batch of dough.

Vineyards are a nice thought, but the text never brings them up. The verse says they surveyed Jazer and Gilead and saw the region was suitable for livestock. These tribes had very large herds and flocks, so livestock is what they had in mind. Vineyards aren't in this verse.

That's the ask. They say, “let this land be given to your servants as a possession. Do not make us cross the Jordan.” (Numbers 32:5). Nice and polite on the front, and then the big request lands. I think I'd be a little nervous asking Moses, Israel's leader, for that one.

That's not what they ask for. They ask for the land of Jazer and Gilead and the other places they name, as a possession, and they say, “Do not make us cross the Jordan.” (Numbers 32:5). So the ask is for this land, not for the best of Canaan. They've picked their spot already.

Twenty or older, that's the line. The LORD says not one of the men twenty years of age or older who came out of Egypt will see the land, with two exceptions He names in the next verse (Numbers 32:11-12). Moses says it was because they did not follow Him wholeheartedly. The oath came with a clear age line.

Eleazar the priest is in this chapter. The Gadites and Reubenites come to Moses, Eleazar and the leaders in Numbers 32:2. But the oath's two exceptions are Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun (Numbers 32:12). Eleazar's just not one of them.

Forty years. The text says He “…made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until the whole generation who had done evil in His sight was gone.” (Numbers 32:13). That's a long stretch, and I think it's a heavy part of the story.

Twelve is a lot shorter than what the text says. It's forty years of wandering in the wilderness, until the whole generation who had done evil in His sight was gone (Numbers 32:13). The number is bigger than most people want to wait.

Moses doesn't hand out any leadership role here. He says that once the land is subdued, they may return and be free of obligation, and the land will belong to them as a possession (Numbers 32:22). Their promise was to go ahead of the Israelites, and the reward is going home with the land they asked for. No trophy, just the land.

False is right. Moses says, “But if you do not do this, you will certainly sin against the LORD—and be assured that your sin will find you out.” (Numbers 32:23). It's a serious line, so he says it plainly. He wants them to know exactly what's at stake in keeping their word.

They don't ask for any time. They answer Moses: “Your servants will do just as our lord commands.” (Numbers 32:25). The text gives no pause and no request to think it over. They simply say they'll do it.

Half isn't what they say. They tell Moses, “…every man will cross over to the battle before the LORD, just as our lord says.” (Numbers 32:27). They say their men are equipped for war, and every one will cross. Their children, wives and livestock are the ones who remain in the cities of Gilead (Numbers 32:26).

Manasseh is right. Moses gives the land to the Gadites, the Reubenites and “…the half-tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph…” (Numbers 32:33). So it's only half of Manasseh that's named in this gift. It's a tribe cut in two.

Nobody gets put to work here. The text says the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh went to Gilead, captured it, and “…drove out the Amorites who were there.” (Numbers 32:39). Capture, then drive out. That's the report.
